Ayapaneco

Ayapaneco refers to a language and community associated with Ayapa in Jalpa de Méndez, Tabasco. Also called Ayapa Zoque or numde 'oode, the language belongs to the Mixe-Zoque family. Community authors, teachers and media projects provide a fuller introduction than sensational stories about a disappearing language and its supposedly last speakers.

Names & relationshipsAyapaneco names a language and associated community in Ayapa; it is a particular member of the Mixe-Zoque family. Language transmission, community membership and the broader Zoque label are related but separate matters.
An expanded introduction, with sources reviewed.This profile develops several themes through identified sources. Citations connect each section to its evidence; remaining gaps appear below. It has not been reviewed or endorsed by the community.
01

Ayapa and the language's names

Ayapa lies on Tabasco's Gulf coastal plain, near the Cuxcuxapa River, in a region shaped by cacao cultivation and contact among Zoque, Nahua, Chontal and other populations. Ayapaneco is also called zoque-ayapaneco or Ayapa Zoque; numde 'oode, numdi oode and numte oote appear in different publications. These spellings refer to the language, not separate peoples. Linguist Jhonnatan Rangel places it in the Mixe-Zoque family and treats interrupted transmission as a specific linguistic challenge.

Read the sources [1] Instituto Nacional de los Pueblos Indígenas [2] Jhonnatan Rangel / Language Technologies for All

02

Community life beyond speaker counts

INPI's account describes a community with agricultural work, trades, shops, professional employment and migration to regional cities. Cacao remains part of foodways through drinks such as pozol and chorote. Patron-saint celebrations create occasions for local and neighboring communities to gather, with San Miguel especially significant. These practices connect livelihood, food and collective identity. They also show why the number of fluent speakers cannot stand in for the number of community members or the extent of their cultural life.

Read the sources [1] Instituto Nacional de los Pueblos Indígenas

03

Reading work by named community authors

Las partes del cuerpo humano en ayapaneco was published in 2013 under the authorship of Manuel Segovia and José Manuel Segovia, with other Ayapaneco speakers credited as collaborators. It combines an introduction, discussion of sounds and writing, illustrated vocabulary and a glossary in Ayapaneco, Spanish and English. The introduction explicitly notes that spelling was not standardized at publication. This makes the book both a practical learning resource and evidence of community authorship, while warning against treating its orthography as timeless or universally fixed.

Read the sources [3] Manuel Segovia and José Manuel Segovia / Instituto Nacional de Lenguas Indígenas

04

Public teaching and language celebration

INALI's report of the first Ayapaneco language festival in May 2013 describes workshops with schoolchildren, poetry, theater, music and traditional games in Ayapa. Materials about the body and a collection of legends were prepared with speakers and distributed during the event. The report recognizes several named contributors, including Manuel Segovia, Isidro Velásquez and Cirilo Velásquez. This dated account documents collaborative teaching and public recognition; it does not establish the size or results of any program in 2026.

Read the sources [4] Instituto Nacional de Lenguas Indígenas

05

Ayapanet and access to recorded knowledge

A contribution by Rangel with the independent community collective Retoño de mis Raíces describes documentation and revitalization work since 2012. Their Ayapanet project responds to a practical problem: audiovisual materials existed, but local infrastructure made them difficult to use. They proposed a low-cost media library accessible through a local wireless network without internet. The contribution describes a testing phase, not a completed universal service. Its emphasis is community control over content and access, alongside education and language learning.

Read the sources [5] Jhonnatan Rangel with Retoño de mis Raíces / Universidad Popular

06

Understanding endangerment without the media shortcut

Daniel Suslak's 2011 article examines the circulation and consequences of the story that Ayapaneco was dying because two speakers refused to talk to one another. Its abstract traces publicity through institutions and international media. That anecdote cannot replace the documented work of multiple contributors. Rangel's research identifies limited documentation, costly annotation, scarce equipment and unreliable connectivity as obstacles, and links language work with inequality and discrimination. These structural conditions give a more useful context for understanding revitalization needs.

Read the sources [6] Daniel F. Suslak / American Anthropologist [2] Jhonnatan Rangel / Language Technologies for All [3] Manuel Segovia and José Manuel Segovia / Instituto Nacional de Lenguas Indígenas
